hints: List what changes from $\text{Na}$ (11) to $\text{Ar}$ (18) in terms of protons added and which principal shell the outer electron is removed from.
Think how adding protons with almost no extra shielding changes the pull of the nucleus on the outer electron.
walkthrough:
Picture what is the same across the period**
You are moving from $\text{Na}$ ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^1$) to $\text{Ar}$ ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6$). The outer electron removed is always from the n = 3 shell, and the inner $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$ shielding electrons are essentially the same. So distance and shielding do not change much.

Picture what is increasing**
Each step adds one proton to the nucleus, so nuclear charge rises from +11 to +18. With the same shielding, the effective pull felt by the outer electron gets stronger and stronger.

Link stronger pull to ionisation energy**
First ionisation energy is the energy for $\text{X(g)} \rightarrow \text{X}^{+}\text{(g)} + e^{-}$. A stronger nuclear attraction holds the outer electron more tightly, so more energy must be supplied to remove it. That is why the general trend rises.

Final answer: Across Period 3 nuclear charge / number of protons increases while shielding stays approximately constant as electrons are added to the same shell.
Nuclear attraction for the outer electron increases, so more energy is needed to remove the electron.

hints: Write the outer configurations for $\text{Mg}$ (12) as $3s^2$ and $\text{Al}$ (13) as $3s^2 3p^1$ and ask which subshell loses the electron.
Compare the energy and shielding of a $3p$ electron with a $3s$ electron in the same shell.
Write the $3p$ configurations for $\text{P}$ (15) as $3p^3$ with three unpaired electrons and $\text{S}$ (16) as $3p^4$ with one pair.
Think what happens to repulsion and ease of removal when two electrons are forced to share the same $p$ orbital.
walkthrough:
Spot the Mg to Al change in subshell**
$\text{Mg}$ is $[\text{Ne}]3s^2$ and $\text{Al}$ is $[\text{Ne}]3s^2 3p^1$. Ionisation removes the outermost electron, so you remove a $3s$ electron from $\text{Mg}$ but a $3p$ electron from $\text{Al}$. Do not treat them as the same shell means the same energy, subshell matters.

Explain why 3p is easier to remove**
The $3p$ orbital is slightly higher in energy than $3s$ and is shielded by the $3s^2$ electrons as well as the inner shells. It is further out on average and feels less net attraction, so it needs less energy to remove. That gives the dip at $\text{Al}$ despite the higher nuclear charge.

Spot the P to S change in pairing**
$\text{P}$ is $[\text{Ne}]3s^2 3p_x^1 3p_y^1 3p_z^1$ with three unpaired electrons in separate orbitals. $\text{S}$ is $[\text{Ne}]3s^2 3p^4$, so one $3p$ orbital now contains a pair. Draw the three boxes to see this clearly.

Explain why pairing lowers IE**
Two negative electrons in the same orbital repel each other. This pair repulsion pushes one electron out more easily, outweighing the increase in nuclear charge from $\text{P}$ to $\text{S}$. So less energy is needed to remove the paired electron from $\text{S}$.

Final answer: From $\text{Mg}$ to $\text{Al}$: the outer electron removed from $\text{Al}$ is in a $3p$ orbital whereas for $\text{Mg}$ it is in $3s$. The $3p$ electron is higher in energy / more shielded by the $3s$ electrons, so less energy is needed to remove it.
From $\text{P}$ to $\text{S}$: $\text{S}$ has a pair of electrons in a $3p$ orbital. Electron pair repulsion makes one electron easier to remove, so IE falls.

hints: Identify $2$, $10$ and $18$ as $\text{He}$, $\text{Ne}$ and $\text{Ar}$ and check from the graph whether IE falls down this group.
Think what happens to distance of the outer electron and number of shielding shells from $n=1$ to $n=2$ to $n=3$.
walkthrough:
Read the group trend**
Atomic numbers 2, 10 and 18 are the noble gases $\text{He}$ ($1s^2$), $\text{Ne}$ ($2s^2 2p^6$) and $\text{Ar}$ ($3s^2 3p^6$). The graph shows a clear fall: $\text{He}$ highest, then $\text{Ne}$, then $\text{Ar}$. So you are explaining a down a group fall.

Balance charge against shielding and distance**
Nuclear charge does increase, but each new noble gas adds a full new principal shell. The outer electron is further from the nucleus and is shielded by more inner electrons. The result is less net attraction, so the outer electron is held less tightly and IE decreases.

Final answer: First ionisation energy decreases from $\text{He}$ to $\text{Ne}$ to $\text{Ar}$ due to decreasing nuclear attraction for the outer electron.
Increasing number of shells / shielding and increasing distance of the outer electron from the nucleus outweigh the increase in nuclear charge.

hints: Recall that $\text{Na}$ and $\text{Mg}$ are both metals, so melting involves breaking metallic bonding between cations and delocalised electrons.
Compare $\text{Na}^{+}$ with one delocalised electron per atom to $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ with two, including charge and ionic size.
walkthrough:
Name what is broken on melting**
Both $\text{Na}$ (11) and $\text{Mg}$ (12) are metallic lattices of cations in a sea of delocalised electrons. Melting loosens this lattice, so melting point reflects the strength of metallic bonding, not covalent or intermolecular forces.

Compare the bonding ingredients**
$\text{Na}$ contributes $\text{Na}^{+}$ + one delocalised $e^{-}$ per atom. $\text{Mg}$ contributes $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ + two delocalised $e^{-}$ per atom, and $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is smaller and has double the charge and higher charge density. More electrons plus higher cation charge means much stronger electrostatic attraction, so more thermal energy is needed and melting point rises sharply.

Final answer: More energy is needed to break the stronger metallic bonding in $\text{Mg}$.
$\text{Mg}$ has more delocalised electrons per atom and smaller, more highly charged $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ ions than $\text{Na}^{+}$, giving stronger attraction between cations and delocalised electrons.

hints: Think why going from $2+$ to $3+$ and adding a third delocalised electron gives a smaller proportional gain than going from $1+$ to $2+$.
walkthrough:
See why the gain levels off**
Going $\text{Na}^{+}$ to $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ doubles the charge and doubles the delocalised electrons, a huge jump in attraction. Going $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ to $\text{Al}^{3+}$ is only a 2+ to 3+ change with a smaller contraction in ionic size, and the $3+$ nucleus holds its electrons so strongly that the third electron is less fully delocalised. So the extra bonding strength, and the rise in melting point, is much smaller.

Final answer: The increase in charge density / attraction is proportionally smaller from $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ to $\text{Al}^{3+}$ than from $\text{Na}^{+}$ to $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ / the size decrease is smaller / not all three electrons in $\text{Al}$ are fully delocalised as nuclear attraction is too strong.

hints: Read the graph values for 15 to 18 and describe the shape, noting the small rise from $\text{P}$ to $\text{S}$ then fall to $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{Ar}$.
Recall that $\text{P}_4$, $\text{S}_8$, $\text{Cl}_2$ and $\text{Ar}$ are all simple molecular or atomic with only weak intermolecular forces to break on melting.
Link the strength of London dispersion forces to the total number of electrons in each molecule or atom.
walkthrough:
State the pattern accurately**
Look at atomic numbers 15 ($\text{P}$), 16 ($\text{S}$), 17 ($\text{Cl}$), 18 ($\text{Ar}$). The graph rises slightly from $\text{P}$ to $\text{S}$ then falls to $\text{Cl}$ and to $\text{Ar}$ lowest. So the order is $\text{S}_8 > \text{P}_4 > \text{Cl}_2 > \text{Ar}$. Saying simply decreases loses the $\text{P}$ to $\text{S}$ rise.

Name the force that controls melting here**
After $\text{Si}$, the structures switch to simple molecules: $\text{P}_4$, $\text{S}_8$, $\text{Cl}_2$, plus single $\text{Ar}$ atoms. No covalent or metallic bonds are broken on melting, only weak London dispersion forces between the molecules. That is why all these melting points are very low compared with $\text{Si}$.

Connect electrons to force strength**
London forces get stronger with more electrons because the electron cloud is larger and more polarisable. Count them: $\text{S}_8$ has $8 \times 16 = 128$ electrons, $\text{P}_4$ has $4 \times 15 = 60$, $\text{Cl}_2$ has $2 \times 17 = 34$, $\text{Ar}$ has 18. The order of electron count exactly matches the order of melting points.

Final answer: Melting point increases from $\text{P}$ to $\text{S}$ then decreases to $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{Ar}$ ($\text{S}_8 > \text{P}_4 > \text{Cl}_2 > \text{Ar}$).
Melting depends on strength of van der Waals / London dispersion forces between molecules (atoms for $\text{Ar}$).
Greater number of electrons per molecule gives stronger dispersion forces and higher melting point, so $\text{S}_8$ (128 $e^{-}$) > $\text{P}_4$ (60 $e^{-}$) > $\text{Cl}_2$ (34 $e^{-}$) > $\text{Ar}$ (18 $e^{-}$).

hints: Recall the structure type of silicon (14) compared with metals on its left and simple molecules on its right.
walkthrough:
Spot the special structure**
Element 14 is silicon, which forms a diamond-like giant covalent network where every $\text{Si}$ atom is covalently bonded tetrahedrally to four others. Melting means breaking these strong $\text{Si-Si}$ covalent bonds throughout the lattice, not just weak metallic or dispersion forces. That needs far more thermal energy, so its melting point towers above the rest of Period 3.
Final answer: $\text{Si}$ has a giant covalent lattice with many strong covalent bonds that must be broken to melt, requiring very large energy.
